Mr. Speaker, before the orders of the day are called, I would like to make a suggestion to the right hon. the Prime Minister with respect to the proceedings of the delegation which waited upon the government and upon parliament this morning. The occasion was rather a memorable one, not only on account of the very great number of delegates, but also on account of the force and earnestness with which they presented their views, as well as on account of the great ability with which those views were put forward. The occasion, I may say, was also a memorable one to myself, for another reason, that it was the only occasion since 1896 on Which I have seen the treasury benches occupied toy gentlemen in whom I had complete confidence. But the suggestion I desire to make is this. We do a good deal of printing in connection with the proceedings of parliament. Some of this printing does not really subserve any useful purpose afterwards, the documents being piled up and stacked away, and not put to very much use. But it would seem to me that the proceedings of this morning, the addresses that were made, the resolutions that were submitted to the government, and as I understand to parliament as well, and the reply of the right hon. the Prime Minister, might very well be printed, so that they would be available for the use of members, and also perhaps to some extent for distribution throughout the country, so far as they might be required by persons interested in the matters of public interest which were discussed by the delegation and toy the right hon. gentleman. I do not know whether the government made anv arrangement to

have the proceedings reported. I observed that there was one of the ' Hansard ' stenographers taking shorthand notes. 1 do not know whether that was for the government or not ; but, in any case, as practically all the addresses were in manuscript, there would be no difficulty at all about securing the necessary material for making a complete report. I would, therefore, urge as this delegation addressed itself not only to the government but to parliament, that the House should pass an order for the the printing or 20,000 or 25,000 copies of the proceedings, which would thus be available for the purpose to which I have already referred, and I earnestly hope that the government will act on my suggestion.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The matter is well worth consideration, I shall look into it.

speechtext: (Translation.) Mr. Speaker, before the orders of the day are called, I wish to bring up a question of privilege, and to protest against an item more or less insulting to me, which appeared in ' Le Soleil ', of the 13th instant, and which is absolutely untrue. Here it is:

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
topic
maintopic: MR. ARTHUR GILBERT, MEMBER EOR DRUMMOND AND ARTHABASKA, RECEIVES A MESSAGE ADDRESSED TO MR. PHILEMON GILBERT AND RETURNS IT ONLY SEVERAL DAYS AFTERWARDS.

speakerposition: subtopic
maintopic: MR. ARTHUR GILBERT, MEMBER EOR DRUMMOND AND ARTHABASKA, RECEIVES A MESSAGE ADDRESSED TO MR. PHILEMON GILBERT AND RETURNS IT ONLY SEVERAL DAYS AFTERWARDS.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Ottawa, 13th.-From the ' Soleil's 5 correspondent.-That poor Mr. Arthur Gilbert, the Conservative - Libera 1-Indepen dent-Nationalist-autonomist representative of Drummond and Arthabaska, is going from bad to worse. After that frigid welcome in the House, after his meaningless speech and his inconsistent voting, he now becomes the hero in a gruesome episode which nevertheless has its comical side.
Thursday last, a message was handed to the hon. member. It bore the signature of Mr. Poirier, and imparted the news of the decease of Mr. Gilbert's mother, the funeral to take place on the Saturday following. Mr. Gilbert was not slow in leaving Parliament House and reaching the railway station, and, greatly moved, proceeded to his home. He was surprised not to see any crape hanging at the door, and still more so to find his mother smiling and in good health. The member suspected some gruesome joke and resolved on finding out the author. Accordingly the message was resorted to once more, and to the surprise of all it was found to have been sent from a place in Beauce, to Mr. Philemon Gilbert, a messeneger in the House of Commons. Besides the sender, Mr. Poirier, is utterly unknown to the member. The iat-ter spent the rest of the week at home and it is only on his return, last night, that he returned the message to the compa ny, whence it was transmitted at once to Mr. Philemon Gilbert. The astonishment and grief of the unfortunate messenger on learning the sorrowful news of the deacease of his mother, two days after the funeral, may be readily perceived.
It is" expected that further developments will take place and that the member will be called upon to explain how he failed to catch the meaning of the message and why he retained it in his possession such a long time unmindful of the feelings of his namesake.
Mr. Speaker, I protest strongly against the falsehoods contained in this item. Here are the facts in regard to the piece of news which appeared in ' Le Soleil ' on December 13. On December 8t,h, at 11 p.m., I found in my room a telegram to my address. That telegram conveyed the news of my mother's decease. I was not taken by surprise at this sad news, seeing that my mother was seriously ill, and had been given up by her physicians. Of course I boarded th'e first train homeward bound. On reaching Montreal, a telegram inform-me that my mother was living. I then returned to the House of Commons the telegram which had been sent to me on Lau-rier avenue. It was not four days afterwards that I returned that message, but on December 9 at 2 p. m., realizing that there
might be some other person by the name of Gilbert in the House of Commons.
Now, I shall read to the House a letter received from the Great North-Western Telegraph Company, through which the' telegram was sent:
Ottawa, Ont., Dec. 15, 1910. Arthur Gilbert, Esq., M.P.,
House of Commons,
City.
Dear Sir,-In answer to your request to find out the date on which you returned the message from St. Joseph de Beauce, addressed to A. P. Gilbert, House of Commons, and which was delivered to you by error, I may say that our office in Montreal advised us at 2.30 p.m. on December 9, that you had returned the message to the company, giving as a reason that the message had not been delivered to the proper address.
Hoping that these explanations will be found satisfactory.
I remain, your truly,
CHARLES E. DAVIS, Mgr.
Such are, Mr. Speaker, the facts exactly as they occurred.
Now, I have always acted as a gentleman, and to my mind, it is a shame for our country that such newspapers should be published.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to call the attention of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to a news item which appears in the ' Victoria Daily Colonist ' of Saturday, December 10, relating to American fish poachers off the west coast of Vancouver island. The item reads in part:
POACHERS OFF WEST COAST. United States Fishing Vessels engage freely within Three Mile Limit off Vancouver Island without Molestation.
Use West Coast Ports as Depots.
Men from Poachers Land with Rifles, use Pitlamps after Nightfall to Hunt Deer-
.	Necessity of Fishery Protection.
American poachers are thick on the west coast; even proceeding up Kyuquot and other sounds after herring and landing hunters on shore who use pit lamps at night when after deer, according to arrivals by the steamer ' Tees.' The poachers ply unmolested and are seemingly in no fear of molestation; for there is no fishety protection off the island coast. For months it seems they have been in undisputed possession of the fishing grounds off the west coast of Vancouver Island, reaping a rich harvest, not only of halibut, but also of cod and herring. The poachers go freely within the three-mile limit. They make Kyuquot sound and Friendly cove their depots. Two or three of the poaching vessels may be seen at anchor in one of these ports from the steamer ' Tees ' on any trip.
On the trip of the ' Tees ' from which she has just returned the steamer proceeded to

Kyuquot. When rounding Raphael point, on her way out of Clayoquot sound, last Monday morning officers and passengers were surprised to see a string of lights extending from Raphael point to Estevan. They resembled the street lights of a city. In the darkness Capt. Gillam made out eight poaching vessels lying well inside on the shoreward side -of his course toward Estevan point.
I do not propose to read the whole article but I wish to quote a few more words:
The poaching vessels do not seem to have any fear of the ' Kestrel.' They seem to be well informed of her movements. At rare intervals the fishery protection steamer visits the west coast and may be seen steaming on a calm day, floating her blue ensign. The west coast settler knows, however, that the poachers wait outside the three-mile limit until her cruise is over, knowing it will be some months before she is seen again off the Vancouver Island coast. The settler on the island coast is chagrined to see how impudently the poachers work, looting the Canadian fishing grounds.
I wish to call the attention of the minister to that and also to the fact that in his report for the last year he states that the fisheries on Hecate Straits have been practically fished out and from previous reports I may say that if they have been fished out there is no question that it has been fished by American poachers. I submit that if the department were aware in 1909-10 that for the first time our fishermen were working along the west coast of Vancouver Island, it was time the protection service should protect that coast and go there more frequently than once in two or three months. We have on that coast five or six fishery protection vessels. If they cannot take care of the west coast of Vancouver Island, particularly when the minister's deputy knew that that coast was being exploited, I say there is something wrong with the Fisheries Department and I trust the minister will take the matter into his consideration, and give the needed instructions in order that it may be attended to.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I desire to call attention to. an item which appears in the Ottawa ' Free Press ' of December 13, very similar to the one which has just been complained of. The item reads:

speakerposition: topic
maintopic: SLIPPERY POACHERS GOT AWAY WHEN OFFICIALS WERE SOUNDLY SLEEPING.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
They had been Trapped, had Surrendered and then got away.
An interesting story of poaching in Canadian waters by United States fishermen with a dramatic sequel has reached the Fisheries Department from Inspector Duncan, of Sault Ste. Marie.
Mr. BARNARD
He reports that on November 16, after the patrol boat ' Kathleen ' had been laid up for the winter, he received information that two American launches were fishing around Parisian island, on the Canadian side of Whitefish bay.
Fight with Rifles.
He notified the fishery officer of the Ontario government, who hired a tug, and after facing a heavy sea the two finally reached the island. They found that one of the launches had managed to get a tip and had escaped to the United States waters, but the other was still on the Canadian side, and there ensued a lively fight with rifles, which resulted in the Americans beaching their launch and escaping into the bush on the island.
The officers waited around a day and a night after taking possession of the launch, which they floated and lashed to their tug. Then, not wishing to leave the two poachers to stay on the island all winter, they left a note ashore stating that if they would surrender they would be given convoy to the mainland.
Let them sleep.
A few hours later the fugitives gave themselves up and were given a place to sleep in the bow of the boat. Then came the sequel.
In the dead of night they made their way to the stern of the tug, skipped aboard their launch, cut it adrift, and when dawn came there was the tug, but the launch and poachers were non est. Presumably thev made their way to home waters without difficulty.
If our protective service is _ of_ as little effect as this would indicate it is a very serious matter. We have complained, time after time, about the manner in which the Americans have invaded our waters. In a case of this kind, where they have been taken red-handed, I think the Minister of Marine and Fisheries might well investigate to find out what the officers were doing that they allowed the men to escape in this manner.

Before you leave the Chair, Mr. Speaker, there is a matter I would like to bring to the attention of the House and the government. I refer to an item which appears in the Ottawa ' Free Press ' of December 1. The heading of the article is: 'Will Knock Out Home Rule if Tory Campaign Wins.' The part of this article to which I direct the special attention of the House begins: * Revolution in Ireland. Funds are being collected to buy arms.'
Now, Sir, if there is going to be a revolution in Ireland for any cause whatever, I regard it as a matter of very great importance.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
speechtext: The motion is for Committee of Supply.

I think I am in order, Mr. Speaker. If there is going to be a revolution in- Ireland I think that justifies us in Canada in believing that there must be some sort of crisis, some emergency which must be met. Now, the question arose in my mind how best we could meet an emergency of this kind. And it naturally occurred to me, after what has been going on for the past month in this House, that the
best way to meet it would be to call out our navy. And I am going to make one or two suggestions to the Prime Minister and his cabinet in that regard, if I may do so. My suggestion is to call out the navy. I see that we spent some $75,000 or $100,000 in wireless telegraphy. I would bring the ' Rainbow ' over to the Atlantic coast. I would line up our navy in St. John harbour-I think that is, perhaps, the best place, because, I understand, a certain George McAvity, who obtained some little consideration from the government for the making of that harbour, wishes to give the boys a send-off. I would line them up in the harbour, and after George McAvity's send-off I would start them off with the ' Montcalm ' ahead, bearing the admiral's flag, and with our friend the Minister of Marine (Mr. Brodeur) on board.
Carried.

I said the 'Montcalm ' carry the flag. I do not know what else is ' carried ' so far. If my hon. friend from Yukon (Mr. Congdon) and other hon, members over there think to carry me off my feet they are much mistaken. I have heard of the scout boat ' Minnie M,,' which has proved very useful to the Liberal party in some parts of this Dominion.
She has gone out of service.

I would bring her back to service. We have her in a class by herself-she is a vote-destroyer, which is a little different from other destroyers. At the wheel of the ' Minnie M.' I would have Capt. Sullivan, and as supercargo I would have our hon. friend the member for Thunder Bay and Rainy River (Mr. Conmee), who is supposed to be a pasrmaster in specials and specialties for campaign purposes. Next to the ' Minnie M.' I would line up the ' Niobe ' and the ' Rainbow,' loaded down with horse marines equipped with Ross rifles of the newest pattern and furnished with emergency rations. I would have on board one of these vessels the Minister of Militia (Sir Frederick Borden), and I would give him his choice whether he would rather be on the ' Niobe ' or on the ' Rainbow.' And, on the sister ship I would have as a stowaway the Solicitor General (Mr. Bureau). I would take him with the fleet for the purpose of making settlement of campaign claims. That is something that is not novel to him, as I understand he was lately employed in that particular service on the government side in the Drummond and Arthabaska election.
On one of the vessels I would have the minister-I was going to say from Victoria, I mean the hon. Minister of Mines (Mr. Templeman), as captain of the watch, for he is known for his sleeplessness and vigilance. As a rear guard, I would have the

' Arctic ' outfitted precisely in the same way as it was for the northern expedition among the Esquimaux-not forgetting the ladies' hats. On it I would have in charge our friend the ex-Minister of Agriculture who, as Minister of Agriculture, expends of the people's money $700,000, and is willing to get up and vote for a useless navy, three or four millions per year. On reaching the scene of action I would turn the rear admiral loose on the insurgents and have him tell them in his own way just what he has not done for Canada, while he has been Minister of Agriculture. But I think if he goes into that fully, as only he can do, the revolution will be over, because he will either talk the insurgents to death, or the few who will be left alive will seek safety in flight. If he does this, as I said, he alone can do, I am sure on this side of the House we will forgive him for the many weary hours we have had to sit and listen to him talking. Now I do not think there is anything to prevent this action on the part of the government. All that is necessary, according to the Naval Bill, is to pass an order in council, have a meeting of the cabinet, call out the navy, and parliament being in session, and judging by the way that all motions made by the government have passed this House, parliament will certainly give its consent. I want to point out to you that if this action is taken, it will do a great deal of good, because it will show the people of Canada that this navy, so-called, is not the useless, costly, tin-pot affair that we on this side assert; and it will further show that the loyalty preached by the First Minister and by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, and others behind them, is not the buncomb that we on this side are prone to suspect. I have ventured in a humble way to point out this necessity to the First Minister, and I would ask him to take cognizance of it.

The details of this vote will be found on page 21 of the estimates. There it is stated that there were last year 182 members employed in the department. The number this year is 152. I will give the reasons for the reduction. Of the former number, 36 have been transferred from the department to the Naval Service. Officers who were employed on the hydrographic survey and the wireless telegraph system have been transferred to the Naval Service. Six other have been also transferred from the Department of Marine and Fisheries to the Naval Service, but they were not attached to those services which Mr. CAMPBELL.
I have just mentioned. They have been replaced in the department by six new officers. Amongst these new officers we are going to provide for an assistant to Mr. Adams, the inspector of boilers and machinery. Mr. Adams is a very efficient officer who has been in the service for many years. He has been asking for some time that we should provide him with an assistant, and I think his request should be granted. We also require in the Fisheries Branch a new officer who will look specially after the commercial side of the fisheries, and to help generally in the administration of that branch. This branch of the service has been increasing largely in late years, and we find it necessary to appoint new men. Mr. Venning, who is superintendent of fisheries, has been unwell for some time, and a great deal of his work devolves upon his assistant, Mr. Found, and it is found advisable to appoint a new man.

There is no use to get the House and the country committed to expenditures for what is a new and distinct service under the head of an old department and simply denominate it * Marine and Fisheries/ I _ think the country has a right to see just exactly what the new service is to cost at the head, in the body and all the way through. speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: No, but he had been a member of parliament, and was a very good member of parliament; and I suppose that a man who passes several years in parliament is well qualified to take charge of any department.

I do not know that it is a necessary qualification, according to the Civil Service Act, in a gentleman who is pulled in from the outside and put over the heads of gentlemen who have been in the service for many years. What special qualification had he?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: I do not think it is required by the Civil Service Act that a deputy minister should be appointed from the public service. They have always been taken from outside the service, except in a very few exceptional cases. Mr. Johnston is a very capable man, with a great knowledge of fisheries, and he lived in a part of the country where he had a great deal to do with marine affairs.

speechtext: Both were appointed by order in council at the same time-Mr. Desbarats for the Naval Department and Mr. Johnston for the Marine Department.

What work was there to do in connection with the naval service before these steamships which we purchased arrived in this country?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: There was a great deal tc do. We had first to ^provide for the organization of the department; then we had to look after the organization of the ships themselves on the other side. In that connection Lord Strathcona rendered a great deal of service, but we had to give instructions from the department, and Mr. Desbarats attended to that from the day the law came into force.

The minister knows the importance of the deputy ministership of a department like that of Marine and Fisheries. The bulk of the work of marine and fisheries remains with the Department of Marine and Fisheries and is under the care of the deputy minister The minister knows that that is a most important service, that it comprises a multiplicity of services, every one of which is very important in its way. Did the min-, ister make his selection of a deputy by looking over the field and getting the very best man that could be got in experience, technical ability and the like of that? Was it simply the good of the service that the minister had in view when he appointed the present deputy?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
Certainly. I had been looking around to find the man best suited for the position. Mr. Johnston, as I explained a few minutes ago, had been connected with the public service of Canada as a member of parliament for many years. He had shown when he was a member of parliament a great deal of industry, he was a man of great ability. As I explained there are in the Department of Marine and Fisheries two special branches. The Marine branch and the Fisheries Branch. Mr. Johnston came from the province of Nova Scotia, and was in close touch with the question of fisheries. Since he has been in the department I have found his advice most valuable upon the question of fisheries, and I am sure he will prove one of the best deputy ministers who has ever been in charge of that department. He came from a part of the country which was largely interested in marine affairs and in that respect also he has already proved to me Mr. BRODEUR.
that he is a far better qualified man than I thought he would be. I must state to the House frankly that although I fully recognized at the time that Mr. Johnston would be an able man I never suspected that he would be as able as I find he is. I am glad to bear that testimony to him before parliament.
My hon. friend refers to the fact that he had no technical knowledge. He certainly is not an engineer, but when a man has been a newspaper man, has been for many years studying public questions in the discharge of his duty as a newspaper man, I think that he becomes more competent to administer any department as deputy minister. That is one of the reasons which induced me to make the selection of Mr, Johnston, and I can assure the House from the experience I have had of him so far that he is going to prove one of the best deputy ministers that the Department of Marine and Fisheries ever had.

He certainly was a very useful man here in some respects, and if these qualifications which he possessed and displayed here will be of value in the department he ought to be a very valuable man. He was a splendid man in the Public Accounts Committee in preventing the finding out of anything, or ascertaining how money was spent. He was usually tne handy man in this House for the government whenever they wanted to put up a man to do something or to kill time. That is another qualification, and the third and most important qualification is that he was a defeated candidate whom the people had rejected because they did not think he was fit to represent them-and that makes him more valuable for the department.

Department of Mines-salaries, $213,189.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
There is a proposed increase of 21 officials for next year in the Mr. FISHER.	I
Department of Mines. The deputy minister at present is Mr. Low', who unfortunately for several years has been an invalid. His work is being attended to by the Director of the Geological Survey wrho is Acting Deputy Minister. There is an increase in the Geological Survey branch, and there is an increase in consequence of the occupation at a very early date of the new Geological Museum. The Mines Department has not been in recent years expanding as rapidly as w'e would wish, owing to the inadequacy of the old building. The total increase in the vote is about $27,000. The increase is owing to the appointment of a number of technical officers, and also to the statutory increases of the present officers. The increase in the Mines Department is owing to the fact that the staff in recent years has been altogether inadequate, and we have been unable to meet the demands upon it. We have been hesitating in making appointments during the last year, because of the inadequate accommodation we have had in our old building. We are now being provided with better quarters, and we desire to bring the staff up to its proper number to meet the requirements. Appointments are all made under the Civil Service Act.
How many have been appointed during the last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Very few.
Were there any promotions?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: We are providing in this estimate for a number of statutory increases. There were very few additions to the staff in either of the branches last year. We have appointed one or two geologists.
What are the officers in the First Division of Subdivision B in the Mines branch, engaged in doing, -where there are five officials?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Mr. Wait is the chief of the chemical division ; Mr. B. Haanel is a mining engineer who has charge of the testing laboratory ; Mr. Frechette is a mining engineer whose business it is to determine the area and size of the iron ore deposits. Dr. Wilson is in charge of the metallurgical branch. Mr McLeish is chief of division of mineral resources and statistics. Mr. Lindman is also a mining engineer, working principally on iron ore deposits.
Are these men engaged all the time at Ottawa?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
No, in the summer they go out and make surveys. Mr. Lindman has been making surveys in the vicinity of Ottawa and in the maritime provinces. He was sent down to Nova Scotia

to determine, as far as he could, the extent and area of the large iron ore-bearing districts. Mr. Wait, who is a chemist, and Mr. McLeish, the statistician, are permanently loqcupied at Ottawa. The other mining engineers are sent out.
What is the chemist doing all the year round?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I presume he is analysing ores of all kinds, his business is to make analysis of all ores. The mining engineer must have his ores analysed. The work in that branch as well as the work in the Geological Survey consists entirely in the analysis of ores, minerals and rocks.
Specimens of which are sent in by the general public?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Yes, and by the Geological Survey staff who are out in the country. The samples which they'bring in are analysed by the chemist, to determine the quality and character of the formations where they have been found. It is absolutely necessary to the work of the department.
Is a person outside at liberty to send in any specimen of ore and have it analysed?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Yes, in the mines branch.
He can demand that, can he?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Well, no, there is a charge. I told Dr. Haanel about a year ago to make that charge a little more than private assayers would charge for the work. We do not want to compete with private assayers, but notwithstanding that there are a great many peetple who want a government assay and we do that work for them.
Of course, a government assay is very valuable.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Yes. I think we have in both branches excellent chemists who do very good work.
Then the public outside is charged for the chemists' work on their ores?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Yes.
Not only charged but charged more than private assayers charge. I hardly think that is fair. The general public prefer a government assay.
It is worth more to them.

It is worth more to them. I think this is one of the things in which governments should help the people instead of simply trying to get 47i
money out of them. Tariff for revenue only should not be the policy on every line.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The charge is very little more, but the reason is that we have in Montreal and Toronto and in other large cities private assayers who are making their living by assaying samples of ore. The government is not especially anxious to emtploy the assay office in competition with these men. We have an assay office for the benefit of the work of the department, but in doing that we find) that there are a great many applications for government assays. These assays are, I believe, preferred by mining men and others; at all events, they have more confidence in government assays; so that we do assaying for any person who has samples.
What was the revenue last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I do not^know, but I do not think it was very much.
I sulppose the hon. gentleman would have the figures available?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I am sure they are.
It would be rather interesting to know what the revenue was.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I can get the figures but I do not think it was very much.
How many (private places are there in Montreal and Ottawa where you can get assays made?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I am advised that there is one in Montreal, and I assume that there will be one in Ottawa. In smaller cities than Montreal and Ottawa there are a number of men engaged in the work of analysis and assay. In Victoria we have one or two making their living by that work, also in Vancouver and Nelson; at least there used to be one in Nelson. I do not know but what my hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson) may think we should do this work for nothing.
I did not say so.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Or for very little.
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
Less probably than the private practitioner demands. If we did that we might require a dozen chemists who might be analysing ores all the time. Plenty of ores that I have analysed at the request of members of this House were perfectly useless. It would be absolutely impossible for us to carry on our work unless we were making a small charge. We do not want to compete with outside assayers, and we think that a man who wants a sample of ore analysed should not

object to paying a dollar more for a government analysis than for a private one.

It is not altogether the price, although the price has a good deal to do with it, but it is the inconvenience. I understand there is only one place where you can get this work done here and one in Montreal. In the county that I live in a man who is out prospecting finds it a very difficult and slow process. If a man is out prospecting and he has some 10, 20 or 30 samples that he wants to have assayed it is a very important matter to him if he is called upon to pay $2 or $3 to get each sample assayed. It means a great deal of money. Prospectors can go over to Belleville, where there is a provincial assay office, but they will probably have to wait two or three weeks to get a return. There are not very many men in Ontario making a business of assaying ores, and if the government had an institution doing the work at actual cost it would be in the interest of the country and of the mining industry. No man out prospecting, however expert he may be, can tell exactly what there is in rocks. It is necessary for him to have an analysis to know. If a man has ten, twenty, thirty or forty samples, if he has to send them to one of these assay offices and has to pay $2 or $3 each it means a very considerable sum. Perhaps some of the samples that he would consider worthless might be the ones that would turn out to be the most valuable. I am not altogether advocating a government assay office, but I think that in the interest of the country and of the mining industry it would be a good thing if one were established.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I am sorry that I have not the schedule of charges for this work, but I can have that information on the main estimates.

I think that the minister's reason for these charges is not a good one. It appears to me that it would be a benefit to the country and to the mining industry if these charges were made merely nominal. I think that is the case with the provincial assay office, and I see no reason why mining men should not be encouraged to send their ore down here for an independent assay as to its value. I think this is a department into which the government might very well go more extensively than it has in the past. As far as private offices are concerned, it is a well known fact to men who have been connected with mining that a great many of the supposed assays they get from these small offices are, to say the least, very misleading. It would be betteT to have an office on a larger scale under an official, where the public could be accommodated at a nominal charge.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue

speechtext: I am somewhat interested in this question. I know a prospector who sent samples to the government assay office and also to private offices to have them assayed. He found that at one office they had practically guessed at it, while at the other place they had made a proper assay.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: That was not at the government office?

No. But the slowness of the government office is what prospectors complain of. If they have to depend on these private offices generally they are not always satisfactory, as they sometimes are merely guessing at it. They send to you a printed report, and it is practically valueless to the prospector.
I would like to ask the minister to tell the House whether he is assisting any drilling operations, in what districts these are being assisted and the amount of money being expended.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The policy of assisting drilling operations which was carried on to a very limited extent two years ago was discontinued over a year ago, and it is not the intention of the department to revive it.
Has the $35,000 voted some years ago- for assisting drilling operations been disposed of?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Some two years ago there was a vote-of $25,000 for drilling for coal in Prince Edward Island. The government thought that as that province had seldom had any money expended in it for geological survey work and as we were anxious to demonstrate whether coal existed there, this vote should be taken, and it was expended for that purpose. There was a vote of $10,000 for drilling in the neighbourhood of Calgary and I think a little in the province of Nova Scotia. That is the last expenditure made by the department for such purpose. I am sorry to say we did not find any coal in Prince Edward Island.
How many wells were drilled in Prince Edward Island and to what depth?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Five, at an average depth of about 2,000 feet.

Was the contract for these wells let by public tender? A return brought down some years ago showed an expenditure of $12,000 and we were waiting until the balance of the $35,000 was expended before making inquiry. This question is worthy of more attention than we can give it now, but let me ask why $25,000 was expended in Prince Edward Island when the minister has given up the idea

of doing such work in Ontario and the western provinces where there is a great deal of work to be done along these lines?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Under the terms of confederation the Dominion government has got to carry on geological survey work in all the provinces. In Prince Edward Island little geological survey work has ever been done, and the provincial government agreed to accept in lieu of it an expenditure of $25,000 by this government to demonstrate whether there was coal in that province. That is the reason and it is an excellent reason. If my hon. friend wishes to move for a return I will be very glad to bring down all the information with regard to the work carried out in Prince Edward Island.
Were tenders called by public advertisement?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: No. The director of the survey received from well known mining engineers the names of contractors for that class of work and he sent an invitation to each one to tender. It was just as good as though published in the newspapers because there are, I believe, very few professional drillers in the country.

Let me tell the minister that he can find expert drillers from Canada who are sent for from Borneo and India and other foreign lands to carry on their operations. In western Ontario, and in my own town particularly, there are to be found the most expert drillers in the world. I can tell the minister that my information is that this drilling was turned over to Yankee drillers who came here with Yankee drilling rigs, while Canadian drillers were walking the streets of Petrolia. Is not that a fact?
Mr. -TEMPLEMAN. I do not know whether that is a fact or not. My recollection is that a contract was given to a driller from the oil regions of western Ontario, whose name I forget at the moment. We had active competition and the price at which the contract was taken was low ; I think too low.
The minister has a patronage list in his department?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: There is no such thing in the Department of Mines. There has not been even a messenger appointed on account of his politics since I took charge.
I was addressing my remarks about the drilling.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The lowest tenderer got the work and I do not know who he is or what his politics are.

Did the minister advertise in the public press for tenders? If not,
I suppose he consulted the patronage list?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: No.

The minister shakes his head, but he admits that he hunted up a certain number of drillers and asked them for a price. The minister tells us he accepted the lowest tender and that part of it is all right, but the other part is all wrong. There are no doubt drillers in the country who are not on the minister's list and they should have a chance to tender.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I think this is the only instance in which the Department of Mines has had tenders for any purpose whatever, so that we have no policy on the subject. We got the names of a number of drillers from mining engineers. I shall be very glad to bring down full particulars if my hon. friend moves for a return. We wanted to deal directly with the practical men who had drilling machines and could do the work, and cut out the middleman.

My hon. friend is evading the question. When he wants some drilling done he selects certain drillers and asks them to tender. I think my hon. friend should substitute a broader policy and call for tenders in a public way by advertisement in the newspapers. Then I do not see that it would make any difference whether the middleman reached the department or not.

The minister talks about there being only a few drilling plants in the country. At the time these contracts were let there were fully 75 drilling rigs operating in western Ontario, and if the minister had publicly advertised for tenders for this work in _ the newspapers he would have avoided this criticism. It was a large expenditure of money, $25,000 in Prince Edward Island and $10,000 in Nova Scotia for drilling, some of it in old holes. Some of these holes had been drilled, if I remember rightly, nearly 2,000 feet, and the contractor went on and completed the depth, and got payment, I suppose, for the whole of it. I would not consider that a business proposition on the part of the minister.
What was the net result of this expenditure?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The net result was that the holes were drilled to a depth of 2,000 feet and no petroleum was discovered.
How much was expended?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue

speechtext: Has my hon. friend given up the drilling business altogether?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Yes.	[DOT]
Does the hon. minister intend to drill any wells in the western provinces? We have great indications of oil in southern Manitoba, and I think it would be a good idea.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: After an experiment of several years, we have concluded that the subsidizing of well-drilling is not a desirable policy. It is not necessary to subsidize well-drilling in the province of Alberta, for instance, as private capital has expended hundreds of thousands of dollars there without asking any government aid. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company has been drilling for natural gas at two or three points, and several other large companies have been drilling for petroleum in southern Alberta, and also, I think, at points in Saskatchewan. Surely nobody would advocate the Dominion government subsidizing the drilling of wells for petroleum in western Ontario. If we ever started that business there would be no end to it. If the expenditure of $25,000, or even $50,000 would demonstrate the existence of a great petroleum field in the western provinces we would not hesitate for a moment to incur the expenditure; but private capital is doing that work, and while it has not been very successful as yet, it may be before long. We could spend a quarter of a million dollars in subsidizing well-drillers all over this country, and it is just because the demands on the department have exceeded the possibility of complying with them, and because of the lack of success we have had from the assistance given, that I determined a year ago to terminate altogether the policy of subsidizing well-drilling.

I think the government got discouraged very easily when they stopped after spending $25,000; yet they expect private capital to go on and explore new fields. In my district there have been a number of private individuals making tests for petroleum. All the surface indications were as good as could be expected, but the great difficulty up to the present has been that the men who undertook the work have been unable to secure capital to go on. In a new field I do not think it would be out of place for the government to do some of that exploration work. $25,000 is a small thing in such an enterprise.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Ten or twelve years ago the government spent a much larger sum in northern Alberta alone, and struck a large gas well. Since that time aid has been given to companies or private individuals drilling wells on their own account. We gave a certain sum per foot after a certain depth. But except on the occasion I have mentioned we have never carried on independent work ourselves.
I understand the minister would not object to assisting in a small way private individuals exploring in a certain district?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Yes, the department will object to any more well-drilling anywhere. It has not worked satisfactorily, it was not encouraging and it would be very invidious to assist in one part of the country -and not in another. If the government are going to bore or assist in the boring of a hole to find petroleum, why should they not assist in running a shaft into a mountain to find a gold reef?
Was there not a vote of $20,000 three or four years ago for this kind of thing?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I do not remember a vote of that size. The largest was $25,000 for Prince Edward Island two years ago We had always had a small sum which we have expended from year to year. I think work has been done in half a dozen places in ten years.
The minister absolutely refuses to -assist in any wellboring.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
Yes.
Department of Labour-salaries, $37,850; contingencies, $13,000.
What is the explanation?

There is a net addition of three clerkships, one in the First Division, Subdivision B, to add a statistician to the department ; one in the Third Division, Subdivision A at $900, a clerk to assist in looking after correspondence, the filing of letters. That work has grown very considerably and up to the present time has taken the services of different-clerks, but I desire to have it under one clerk who will be primarily responsible. There is an increase of two in the staff of stenographic clerks. There was an appropriation voted last year for a clerk in Division 2, Subdivision B, $1,200 which is not being asked for this year.
They will pass the Civil Service examination?
Yes.
How are these selected? Have they all -been appointed?
None have been appointed as yet; if parliament votes the appropriation they will be appointed.
Have they been selected?
They are not selected yet.
Will they be promotions or new officials?

I think two of them may be promotions if the clerks qualify, but of course, they will have to satisfy the Civil Service Commission that they are suitable for the higher position. If they are I would prefer to appoint some one in the department rather than from outside.
Is the work in the department increasing rapidly?

Yes, the work is increasing very considerably.
Department of Trade and Commerce-salaries, $55,912.50; contingencies, $21,500.
Are there any changes in this department?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Nearly all the increases are due to statutory increases. There is one promotion to the First Division, Subdivision B. That is Mr. Lewis, who goes up from the Second Division, Subdivision A. The vacancy in the Second Division is to be filled by a transfer from the outside service at the minimum salary.
I see an item at Y-3 of the Auditor General's Report of $387 for printing books and maps. Where is this printing done?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: That is all in the Printing Bureau.
The minister means through the Printing Bureau Department. It is very likely distributed all over the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
The different departments do not know that at all, they deal with the Printing Bureau entirely.
Office of the Auditor General-salaries, $106,500; contingencies, $6,500.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: As there is no minister in charge of this department, whose duty is it to recommend increases or changes in the staff?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The estimates were prepared by the Auditor General himself.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Does the government follow out his recommendations with regard to increases and changes in the staff?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: So far as I know, yes. Does my hon. friend (Mr. Per-ley) doubt it?

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I am asking for information. There being no minister in charge of the department, the Auditor General being responsible to this parliament alone, I was simply asking whether his recommendations with regard to changes in the staff were -carried out in all cases?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
So far as my memory goes, the recommendations of the
Auditor General have always been accepted. There may have been some difference of opinion as to whether a given change came within the rules of the civil service or not. Otherwise, I believe they are always accepted.

If the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) will make inquiry, I think he will modify his opinion somewhat on that point. The Auditor General has to work through the Minister of Finance, and makes his recommendations the same as any other deputy minister. As a rule, his recommendations come with more force than from a deputy minister, because he is a semi-independent officer. But if the Finance Minister thinks it is improper to give certain increases, he puts his foot down.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not dispute that. But I do not think the present Finance Minister has ever done it. My hon. friend (Mr. Foster) when Minister of Finance may have done it.
I think others have done it. In the Auditor General's Department I see some increases in Class 3 A-provision, made for three more clerkships.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: And there are corresponding decreases in 3 B.
I suppose that means promotions. .

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I suppose so.
Whom is it proposed to promote?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I have not that information.
Will the minister (Mr. Fisher) be kind enough to get that information? I will bring it up on another item.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Yes.
High Commissioner's Office, London-salaries, $12,700; contingencies, $26,180.
There seems to be the same number of clerks. But there is an increase of $4,900 in contingencies. What is the explanation of that?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I cannot give that information.
Better let it stand.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Stand.
Departments generally-Contingencies-care and cleaning of departmental buildings, including amount of $50 each to E. Snowden and W. H. Jeffery for firing noon gun, $63,000.
There is an increase here of $9,000, or exactly one-sixth over the previous year. What is the explanation of that?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I have not the facts before me. Let it stand.
Some resolutions reported.
Sir WILFRID LAURIER moved the adjournment of the House.
Perhaps I ought to ask what will be the duties of to-morrow and next week?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: General enjoyment.
